title: Chlamydia & Mycoplasma: Hides Inside, No Wall Outside
summary: See why the Gram stain misses Chlamydia and Mycoplasma, follow the chlamydial EB–RB life cycle, and choose the right test and specimen — NAAT, the right swab, and why cold agglutinins don’t diagnose Mycoplasma.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 62 Hit 1 (NAAT for C. trachomatis), Hit 2 (EB/RB cycle — sizes not taught), Hit 3 (energy metabolism, corrected: register flag rv-ct-energy), Hit 6 (M. pneumoniae diagnosis; cold agglutinins), Hit 12 (swab types), Traps 1 and 3 and the Figure 62 anchor. Checked against Workowski 2021 (CDC STI guidelines), CDC 2014 laboratory recommendations, Singh 2026, Mandel 2024, Cheong 2023, Mazzulli 2017, Bongiovanni 2026, Zheng 2026 and Raghuram 2025. The reviewer’s Trap 4 treatment line (azithromycin or doxycycline as equals) is logged as rv-ct-regimen and not taught here.

objectives: Describe the chlamydial developmental cycle (EB → RB → EB) and why chlamydiae are obligate intracellular.
Explain why Mycoplasma is not seen on Gram stain and resists β-lactams.
Select NAAT specimens for C. trachomatis and state when culture is still used.
Interpret cold agglutinins and M. pneumoniae molecular results correctly.

scenes.title: Two infections the Gram stain can’t see
scenes.altText: Two specimen cards: a urethral swab from a man with discharge — Gram stain shows white cells but no organisms; and sputum from a teenager with “walking pneumonia” — Gram stain shows nothing useful. Both cards get a “no organisms seen” stamp. A question token asks why.

cues.text: A young man has urethral discharge. The Gram stain shows white cells — but no bacteria.
A teenager has a lingering “walking pneumonia.” Again, the Gram stain shows nothing useful.
Two common infections, both invisible to the Gram stain. One hides inside our cells; the other has no cell wall.

scenes.title: Normal: the chlamydial life cycle
scenes.altText: A host epithelial cell (large card) with a nucleus. A small elementary body (EB) token — infectious, non-replicating — attaches and enters, sitting inside a membrane-bound inclusion. It turns into a larger reticulate body (RB), which divides (more RB tokens appear). RBs then turn back into EBs, which are released to infect new cells. Note: the cycle takes about 2 days (~48–54 h for serovar L2). Energy note: RBs scavenge ATP from the host; EBs can make some ATP — the old “makes no ATP at all” idea is outdated.

cues.text: Chlamydia is an obligate intracellular bacterium. Its infectious form, the elementary body, is small and doesn’t divide. It attaches to an epithelial cell and is taken inside.
Inside a membrane-bound pocket called the inclusion, it turns into a larger reticulate body — the form that divides, again and again.
Then reticulate bodies turn back into elementary bodies, which burst out to infect new cells. One cycle takes about two days.
Reticulate bodies take ATP from the host cell. But the old claim that chlamydiae make no ATP at all is outdated — elementary bodies can make some.

scenes.title: What changes: why routine methods fail
scenes.altText: Left panel, Chlamydia: an agar plate with a cross — obligate intracellular bacteria do not grow on agar; culture needs living cells, is slow and is less sensitive than NAAT. Right panel, Mycoplasma: a cell drawn without a wall layer — no cell wall, so β-lactams (which attack the wall) cannot work, and the organism is not seen on Gram stain. A token: M. pneumoniae does not grow with standard culture methods.

cues.text: Chlamydia multiplies only inside living cells, so it won’t grow on ordinary agar. Culture is slow and specialised, and misses infections that molecular tests find.
So for chlamydia, the lab’s routine answer is a nucleic acid amplification test — a NAAT.
Mycoplasma is different: it has no cell wall at all. So it doesn’t show on a Gram stain, and drugs that attack the wall — like penicillins and cephalosporins — can’t touch it.
Mycoplasma pneumoniae also won’t grow with standard culture methods, so molecular tests do most of the work here too.

scenes.title: In the lab: NAAT, the right swab and what cold agglutinins can’t do
scenes.altText: Specimen chooser for C. trachomatis NAAT: women — vaginal swab (patient-collected is acceptable), cervical swab or first-void urine; men — first-void urine or urethral swab. A card: culture is kept for special cases such as suspected child sexual assault (boys; extragenital sites in girls), where data are insufficient for nonculture tests. Swab card for chlamydia culture: Dacron, cotton or rayon tips on plastic or aluminum shafts; wooden shafts and calcium alginate tips can inhibit growth. M. pneumoniae card: molecular testing of a respiratory specimen, with serology; a positive PCR can reflect carriage; cold agglutinins appear in only 50–75% and are neither sensitive nor specific — not diagnostic.

cues.text: For chlamydia, NAAT is the recommended test. In women, a vaginal swab — even patient-collected — a cervical swab, or first-void urine. In men, first-void urine or a urethral swab.
Culture is kept for special situations, such as suspected sexual assault in children, where nonculture tests haven’t been validated.
If you do culture chlamydia, use Dacron, cotton or rayon tips on plastic or aluminum shafts. Wooden shafts and calcium alginate tips can inhibit growth.

For Mycoplasma pneumoniae, molecular tests on a respiratory sample lead, with serology — though a positive PCR can mean carriage. Cold agglutinins appear in only half to three-quarters of patients and aren’t specific, so they can’t make the diagnosis.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Trap card: “Order chlamydia culture as the routine test” is crossed out → “NAAT is the recommended test; culture for special cases.” Trap card: “High cold agglutinins diagnose Mycoplasma pneumoniae” is crossed out → “Supportive at best; use molecular testing (and serology).” Trap card: “Chlamydiae make no ATP at all” is crossed out → “They rely heavily on host ATP, but EBs can make some.”

cues.text: Trap one: culture isn’t the routine test for chlamydia. NAAT is — culture is kept for special cases.
Trap two: cold agglutinins don’t diagnose Mycoplasma pneumoniae. They’re missing in many patients and appear in other infections.
Trap three: “chlamydiae make no ATP” is an old idea. Reticulate bodies take host ATP, but elementary bodies can make some of their own.

scenes.title: Hides inside, no wall outside
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Chlamydia hides inside; Mycoplasma has no wall — so the Gram stain sees neither, and the NAAT finds both.” A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: Chlamydia hides inside; Mycoplasma has no wall. The Gram stain sees neither — molecular tests find both.

Where it breaks: chlamydia’s problem is where it lives, not a missing wall; a positive Mycoplasma PCR can mean harmless carriage; and other organisms also escape the Gram stain, so this isn’t a rule for every “no organisms seen” result.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Chlamydia: obligate intracellular EB → RB → EB · NAAT is the test”, “Mycoplasma: no cell wall · molecular tests · cold agglutinins not diagnostic”.

cues.text: Chlamydia lives inside cells and Mycoplasma has no wall, so neither shows on a Gram stain — NAAT is the routine test, and cold agglutinins never make the diagnosis.

props.label: Chlamydia: intracellular EB → RB → EB · NAAT is the routine test
Mycoplasma: no cell wall · molecular tests · cold agglutinins not diagnostic

explanation.what: Plain language: chlamydia lives and multiplies inside our cells, and Mycoplasma has no cell wall, so neither shows on a Gram stain and both are usually found with molecular tests. Scientific terms: biphasic developmental cycle — elementary body (EB; infectious, non-replicative) → reticulate body (RB; replicative, within the inclusion) → EB (secondary differentiation), ~48–54 h for serovar L2; Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall.
explanation.why: Obligate intracellular growth means chlamydiae do not grow on agar; culture requires living cells. RBs scavenge host ATP, though EBs can generate some ATP — the 1960s–70s “energy parasite” hypothesis has been challenged. Without a cell wall, Mycoplasma cannot be Gram stained and is untouched by wall-active β-lactams.
explanation.measure: C. trachomatis: NAAT is the recommended test — vaginal (clinician- or patient-collected), cervical or first-void urine in women; first-void urine or urethral swab in men. Culture retained for special situations (e.g., child sexual assault in boys and extragenital sites in girls). Chlamydia culture swabs: Dacron, cotton or rayon on plastic/aluminum shafts; wooden shafts and calcium alginate can inhibit growth. M. pneumoniae: molecular testing (with serology); PCR may reflect carriage; cold agglutinins (50–75% of patients) lack sensitivity and specificity.
explanation.differs: Chlamydia (intracellular; NAAT) vs Mycoplasma (wall-less; molecular testing; slow growth). Cold agglutinins (host IgM, supportive) vs pathogen detection (diagnostic).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: EB vs RB, NAAT as test of choice, culture indications, swab choice, “no cell wall” consequences, and cold agglutinin traps.

right.label: Mycoplasma
points: Molecular tests; cold agglutinins not diagnostic

mnemonic.text: Chlamydia hides inside; Mycoplasma has no wall — the Gram stain sees neither, the NAAT finds both.
mnemonic.explanation: Both escape the Gram stain for different reasons, and molecular tests are the routine route to diagnosis.
mnemonic.limitation: Chlamydia’s issue is location, not a missing wall; Mycoplasma PCR can detect carriage; other organisms also escape the Gram stain.

Treatment, LGV, trachoma and genital mycoplasmas are not covered here.
takeaway: Chlamydia lives inside cells and Mycoplasma has no wall, so neither shows on a Gram stain — NAAT is the routine test, and cold agglutinins never make the diagnosis.

questions.stem: Which chlamydial form is infectious and taken up by a new host cell?

options.rationale: Correct. The non-replicating EB infects cells and then differentiates into an RB.
Incorrect. The RB is the replicating, non-infectious intracellular form.
Incorrect. The inclusion is the membrane-bound compartment where chlamydiae develop.
Incorrect. Chlamydiae do not form spores.

questions.stem: A clinic asks which test to use for routine chlamydia screening in an asymptomatic woman. What should the laboratory recommend?

options.text: NAAT on a vaginal swab (patient-collected is acceptable)
options.rationale: Correct. NAATs are the most sensitive tests and are recommended; patient-collected vaginal swabs are acceptable.

options.text: Chlamydia culture on a cervical swab
options.rationale: Incorrect. Culture is less sensitive and kept for special situations.
Incorrect. Chlamydiae are intracellular and not detected on Gram stain.
Incorrect. Serology is not used to diagnose genital chlamydial infection.

questions.stem: A teenager with atypical pneumonia has a cold agglutinin titer of 1:64. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Supportive but not diagnostic; confirm with molecular testing (and serology)
options.rationale: Correct. Cold agglutinins occur in only 50–75% of M. pneumoniae infections and in other infections.
Incorrect. The test lacks sensitivity and specificity.

options.text: Rules out Mycoplasma because the titer is too low
options.rationale: Incorrect. A negative or low titer never rules M. pneumoniae out.

options.text: Indicates the organism will respond to penicillin
options.rationale: Incorrect. Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall, so β-lactams do not work.

references.usedFor: EBs generate ATP from glucose-6-phosphate and amino acids; RBs scavenge host ATP.

references.citation: Mazzulli T. Laboratory diagnosis of infection due to viruses, Chlamydia, Chlamydophila, and Mycoplasma. In: Long SS, Prober CG, Fischer M, eds. Principles and Practice of Pediatric Infectious Diseases. 5th ed. Elsevier; 2017:1434-1447.e5.

Cold agglutinins develop in only 50–75% of M. pneumoniae infections, lack sensitivity and specificity, and should not be used for diagnosis; serology with culture or PCR is most reliable.

references.citation: Bongiovanni M. From respiratory pathogen to systemic threat: rethinking Mycoplasma pneumoniae infections. Microorganisms. 2026;14(2):419.
references.usedFor: M. pneumoniae lacks a cell wall; respiratory PCR may reflect colonization and serology is delayed.

references.citation: Zheng L, Liu H, Xu C, Song F, Ding S. Macrolide-resistant Mycoplasma pneumoniae in children: clinical features, treatment response, and outcomes in a retrospective cohort from China. Front Pediatr. 2026;14:1812564.
references.usedFor: M. pneumoniae lacks a cell wall and is intrinsically resistant to β-lactams (and aminoglycosides).

references.citation: Raghuram A, Furmanek S, Chandler T, et al. Description of a current outbreak of Mycoplasma pneumoniae in the United States. Pathogens. 2025;14(1):60.
references.usedFor: M. pneumoniae is not detectable on Gram stain (no cell wall) and does not grow with standard culture methods; NAAT is the primary diagnostic method.

claims.text: EB (infectious, non-replicative) → RB in inclusion (replicative) → EB; ~48–54 h (L2).
RBs scavenge host ATP; EBs and C. trachomatis can generate ATP; “energy parasite” hypothesis challenged.
NAAT recommended for C. trachomatis; specimen types by sex; culture for special cases (child sexual assault, extragenital in girls).
Chlamydia culture swabs: Dacron/cotton/rayon on plastic/aluminum; wooden shafts and calcium alginate can inhibit growth.

Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall: not seen on Gram stain, intrinsically β-lactam resistant, no growth on standard culture; NAAT primary; PCR may reflect carriage; cold agglutinins 50–75%, nonspecific, not diagnostic.
Chlamydiae are obligate intracellular (they multiply only inside living cells, not on agar); NAATs are more sensitive than culture.

morphology.note: Cells, elementary and reticulate bodies are schematic tokens, not real inclusion morphology.
